We also study GMM weighting, misspecification, and over-identification testing under finite-population asymptotics. Notably, even though the optimally weighted GMM estimator is infeasible under finite-population asymptotics, the regression adjustment estimator in a randomized controlled trial is shown to be asymptotically equivalent to the optimally weighted GMM estimator. A simulation study and real data application illustrate the usefulness of our GMM theory.

papers.title: Sparsity and uniformity in dynamical Manin--Mumford problems
papers.abstract: For endomorphisms of the complex projective plane of a given degree, we prove that the existence of a special curve of bounded degree, in the sense of the dynamical Manin--Mumford conjecture, is confined to a proper algebraic subvariety of the parameter space. This confirms a conjecture of DeMarco and Mavraki in dimension two. For general regular polynomial endomorphisms of $\mathbb A^k$, we obtain a uniform dynamical Manin--Mumford bound outside an exceptional hypersurface. These results arise from a common strategy, valid in every dimension and codimension, which reduces such questions to the geometry of exceptional loci in the space of pairs formed by subvarieties and maps. We control these loci by combining arithmetic equidistribution, blender constructions, dynamical directions, monodromy arguments, and degenerations at the boundary of parameter space.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Unsupervised Learning for Reliable Beamforming in Cluttered MIMO-ISAC
papers.abstract: In this paper, we consider joint beamforming and power allocation for a mobile multiuser MIMO integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) network with clutter, residual self-interference, and outdated channel state information, under per-user rate and sensing signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) constraints that must hold on every realization. The design must be recomputed every block, and distant or weak targets can make the sensing constraint unmeetable. We propose a physics-informed unsupervised learning (PI-UnSL) network that corrects the analytical design, meets the power and norm constraints exactly by construction, and is conditioned on closed-form interference statistics, spanning the whole tradeoff in one pass. We derive a closed-form sensing SINR at the interference-aware combiner, yielding a necessary range-radar-cross-section-power condition and a priority-independent analytic violation floor, so the problem is intermittently infeasible. We then show that a dual targeting below the attainable floor has no fixed point, and calibrate the label-free objective against the measured floor. Numerical results confirm the floor and the bounded calibrated dual, and show that PI-UnSL substantially raises per-realization joint quality of service over the closed-form baseline, delivers more rate than time-division ISAC at matched detection over most of the tradeoff, and exceeds the reliability of an uncalibrated alternating-optimization solver at a fraction of its latency. More broadly, the physical knowledge given to the network, not its architecture, makes such problems learnable without labels: five architectures fail alike from scratch and perform alike when started from the closed-form design and conditioned on its interference statistics.

papers.title: LexiCan: Lexicographic Canonicalization of Point Clouds for Machine Learning Applications
papers.abstract: Canonicalization resolves the rotational and permutation ambiguity of 3D point clouds by selecting a unique orbit representative, maintaining their geometric information while allowing standard architectures, such as Transformers, to operate on them. Existing canonicalizations, however, exhibit discontinuity jumps on molecular configurations and non-trivial invariance errors in popular molecular datasets, which lead to ambiguity in their representation. To bridge this gap, we introduce LexiCan, a canonicalization that is provably invariant under either $O(3)$ or $SO(3)$, empirically invariant to rotations to within $\sim 10^{-6}$ angstroms on the QM9 and QM-sym molecular datasets, and mitigates discontinuity jumps on QM-sym, while running orders of magnitude faster than an existing canonicalization. Finally, non-invariant models perform better on QM9 property prediction and ModelNet40 shape classification with LexiCan than with that canonicalization.

papers.title: Interpolation in path-connected metric spaces using splines on embedded graphs
papers.abstract: We study a local graph-based interpolation framework for data defined on graph vertices embedded in a metric space. The resulting interpolants are constructed from variational graph splines defined on small neighborhoods, yielding continuous-domain extensions of the graph data. We analyze their behavior through energy estimates, Lipschitz continuity, and stability properties, and compare them with $k$-Nearest Neighbor ($k$NN) interpolation as a natural baseline due to its simplicity and widespread use. Numerical experiments on the manifold of symmetric positive definite matrices illustrate the relative performance of the proposed local interpolation schemes and $k$NN interpolation across varying levels of smoothness and noise.

papers.title: Physics Foundation Models for Efficient Control of Fluid Flows
papers.abstract: We investigate whether a physics foundation model (PFM) pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed for closed-loop fluid-flow control. We construct a PFM-based controller by attaching lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to frozen pretrained representations and train the policy using proximal policy optimization (PPO). We evaluate the approach on HydroGym's two-dimensional Kolmogorov-flow environment using vorticity observations at \(64\times64\) and \(128\times128\) resolutions and Reynolds numbers \(\mathrm{Re}=100\) and \(200\). Across these settings, we compare the frozen PFM controller against a baseline MLP policy trained with the same PPO framework. The PFM controller achieves consistently higher reward while requiring smaller executed action magnitudes over training, indicating improved control performance with reduced control effort. These results provide initial evidence that representations learned through self-supervised next-frame prediction can be transferred directly to closed-loop fluid flow control. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/morph.

papers.title: Closed forms all the way up: the sample variance of four observations
papers.abstract: The distribution function $F(y)=\Pr(S^2\le y)$ of the sample variance $S^2$ of four independent observations is elementary on its entire support for every polynomial parent density on $[0,1]$ (without loss of generality), and we give it in finite closed form for the uniform, Beta$(2,1)$ and Beta$(2,2)$ parents. The support splits at $y = 1/6$, $2/9$ and $1/4$, with the ceiling at $1/3$, all fixed by geometry: in coordinates aligned with the cube diagonal the event $S^2\le y$ is a ball of radius $\sqrt{3y}$, the cube projects to a rhombic dodecahedron, and these are the levels at which the ball reaches its faces, edges and two kinds of vertices. The divergence theorem reduces every moment of the clipped ball to integrals along circular arcs, so each regime closes in algebraic functions of $\sqrt{y}$ and inverse trigonometric functions. For the uniform parent the only non-obvious constant is $K_g = 12\sqrt2\arctan\sqrt2$, proportional to the mean width of the cuboctahedron; the Beta constants are rational expressions in $π$, $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt3$ and $\arctan\sqrt2$, as in the uniform case. At $n = 4$ the normal-theory $χ^2$ recipe used in acceptance testing misplaces the $99$th percentile of $S^2$ by $50\%$ for the uniform parent. For three observations, polynomial parents also give elementary closed forms (arXiv:2609.25333), but two elementary cases in a row do not guarantee a third, and we make no claim beyond $n = 4$.

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware integration of deuterium metabolic imaging with genome-scale metabolic modeling reveals diet-associated feasible-space remodeling in mouse skeletal muscle
papers.abstract: Deuterium metabolic imaging (DMI) measures glucose-derived labeling in vivo, but noisy time courses complicate network-level interpretation. We developed an uncertainty-aware workflow that integrates dynamic DMI data with genome-scale metabolic modeling (GEM) through soft flux constraints. After injection of [6,6'-2H2]glucose, dynamic spectra were acquired from gastrocnemius, soleus, and tibialis anterior muscles of control and high-fat diet (HFD) mice. A hierarchical four-state kinetic model estimated labeling parameters while accounting for shared plasma input, tissue-specific kinetics, voxel-level fluxes, isotope effects, and measurement uncertainty. Because glucose labeling was more reliable than lactate and glutamate/glutamine signals, only two DMI-derived quantities were used as GEM anchors: glucose processing mapped to hexokinase flux, and glucose-derived oxidative entry mapped to mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase flux. Two-sided soft target intervals with weighted penalties defined DMI-compatible feasible regions for each mouse and muscle. Flux variability analysis and sampling assessed changes across reactions and metabolic subsystems. The constraints were compatible with the muscle network and affected feasible activity in glycolysis, lactate metabolism, pyruvate oxidation, the TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and redox pathways. HFD-associated changes differed by muscle: tibialis anterior and soleus showed reduced glucose-linked feasible activity, whereas gastrocnemius showed mixed changes with preserved or increased TCA and redox activity. This framework connects noninvasive tracer imaging with network-level metabolic inference while avoiding strong claims from poorly identified signals.

papers.title: Deformation and Symmetry in Two Hypergeometric Supercongruences
papers.abstract: We prove two supercongruence conjectures of Li--Long--Tu concerning truncated very-well-poised ${}_7F_6(1)$ series and Fourier coefficients of modular forms. The proofs are based on a common deformation method. By deforming the original truncated hypergeometric series to suitable terminating series, we are able to apply classical hypergeometric transformations together with Mishev's $W(D_5)$ symmetry. This reduces both problems to congruences for lower-rank hypergeometric sums that can be treated using the $p$-adic methods of Long--Tu--Yui--Zudilin. Although the two cases require different local arithmetic calculations, their global proof structure is the same. The resulting argument gives a unified explanation of these two supercongruences and suggests that the same deformation-and-symmetry method may apply more broadly.

papers.title: Only What You've Signed up For: Secure Workflows with Constrained Diffusion Agents
papers.abstract: As agentic AI systems take on increasingly complex and consequential tasks, securing them against prompt injection becomes critical. Existing defenses often rely on detecting or reasoning about injected malicious instructions and can therefore remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. Diffusion language models (dLLMs), an emerging framework for language generation, offer a new opportunity for security enforcement: by iteratively refining their sequence wide predictions, they enable broader-scope constraint enforcement throughout generation. This paper introduces Policy-Constrained Diffusion Agents (CoDA), a framework that enforces task dependent security policies directly within the denoising process of diffusion language models. At each denoising step, CoDA projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set, maintaining constraint satisfaction throughout generation. We evaluate CoDA across state-of-the-art diffusion language model families under both static and adaptive prompt-injection attacks. Results demonstrate substantial reductions in attack success rate with competitive task utility and practical inference overhead.

papers.title: CSI-Aging-Aware Functional Split Optimization and KAN-LSTM Prediction for Open-RAN NTN
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study functional-split selection for an Open radio access network (RAN) deployed as a non-terrestrial network (NTN), in which a low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellite hosts the radio unit, so that each candidate split (7.2x, 6, 2) places the RAN at a distinct point of the transparent-to-regenerative axis. We capture the space-ground geometry exactly through an instantaneous link plane, which yields closed-form slant range, elevation, delay, and Doppler for an inclined orbit and a rotating Earth. On this geometry we derive the received-SNR density of the elevation-driven LOS/NLOS mixture channel and, through a split-dependent channel state information (CSI) aging mechanism, an uncoded bit-error-rate (BER) law for each split, establishing that what separates the splits is the freshness of the CSI each brings to its adaptation loops: a loop closed on the ground pays the feeder round-trip and incurs an aging-induced error floor. We formulate split selection as a prefer-centralized feasibility problem over reliability, aging, and fronthaul-capacity constraints, and we show that its exact solution is a closed-form region rule in four state coordinates, validated against exhaustive enumeration without a single mismatch. Because this solution is reactive whereas a split change must be initiated ahead of time, we propose a compact Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN)-LSTM, sized for an edge xApp/rApp, that predicts the split schedule seconds ahead; we show that it attains high schedule accuracy at a sub-percent BER-violation probability and delivers nearly all of the ground-truth policy's goodput, outperforming naive and reactive baselines.

papers.title: UDHRBench: Benchmarking Human Rights in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in contexts requiring adherence to ethical and legal norms, yet their alignment with internationally recognized human rights standards remains underexplored. We introduce UDHRBench, a large-scale benchmark for operationalising the evaluation of large language model compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The dataset comprises 1,124 human rights confronting questions covering all 30 articles and 4,496 responses from four large language models (ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, and Fanar), manually annotated by experts for alignment, with high inter-annotator agreement ($κ= 0.801$). Our analysis reveals systematic and non-trivial misalignments, showing that violations typically arise through seemingly rational reasoning: appeals to efficiency, risk management, or scientific neutrality, rather than explicit rejection of rights. We further propose an LLM-as-a-Judge framework for automated evaluation using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, achieving 89.8\% weighted F1-score in detecting human-rights misalignment, alongside a novel Alignment Leniency Score that quantifies how judge models resolve ambiguous cases. The dataset, annotations, and code will be released as open-source resources (https://sina.birzeit.edu/UDHRBench).

papers.title: Fuglede--Kadison Determinants of Shifted Matrix Semicircles
papers.abstract: We prove a variational formula for the Fuglede-Kadison determinant of a self-adjoint matrix semicircle $S_a = a \otimes 1 + \sum_j A_j \otimes s_j$ with deterministic mean $a$. For every real $z$, $\log Δ(S_a - z) = -1/2 + \inf_b F_z(b)$, where the infimum is over positive definite matrices $b$ such that the map $X \mapsto bXb - \sum_j A_j X A_j$ is positive semidefinite, and $F_z$ is an explicit geodesically convex function. Both sides equal $-\infty$ exactly when $z$ is an atom of the spectral measure. The formula was proposed, without proof, in a recent post of Speicher. In the centered case $a=0$ it gives a new proof of the Mai-Speicher capacity formula, and by hermitization it yields a finite-dimensional variational formula for the logarithmic potential of the Brown measure of an arbitrary matrix-valued semicircular element. The proof identifies the determinant with the value of the Dyson action at its critical point and rewrites this critical-point problem as a saddle problem in three matrix variables. For a spectral parameter $z + i\varepsilon$ in the upper half-plane, eliminating two of the variables gives a geodesically convex minimization whose global minimizer is the positive factor $b_\varepsilon$ in a symmetric unitary factorization of the matrix Cauchy transform. The formula on the real axis follows by letting $\varepsilon \to 0$ in the optimal values, with no compactness assumption on the minimizers. At points where the boundary value of the Cauchy transform is nondegenerate, the scales $b_\varepsilon$ converge and the infimum is attained at their limit; this minimizer lies on the boundary of the feasible set when $z$ is in the support of the spectral measure and in its interior when $z$ is in the resolvent set.

papers.title: Word-Aligned Prosody Reflects Speaker Differences More Than Depression or PTSD Severity
papers.abstract: Word-aligned prosody is increasingly used to detect depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), yet the stability and clinical relevance of these measurements remain unclear. We examine stability at two levels. At the word level, we ask whether a speaker produces the same word in a similar speaker-specific way across different utterance contexts. At the speaker level, we ask whether averaging prosody across many words produces consistent speaker scores across separate recordings. Drawing on principles of psychological measurement, we compare these representations in four corpora spanning acted, spontaneous, and clinical speech. Word-specific deviations show little cross-context recurrence (0.01-0.16), whereas speaker summaries are highly consistent, reaching 0.997 in ESD, 0.73-0.90 in MSP-Podcast, and 0.84-0.996 in DAIC-WOZ and PTSD-STOP. Despite this consistency, associations with depression or PTSD severity do not exceed 0.15; equivalence tests exclude effects of 0.30 in all analyses and 0.20 in DAIC-WOZ, while within-person associations with daily PTSD symptoms are near zero ($|ρ|\leq0.04$). Thus, aggregation yields stable speaker-level prosodic measures, but these measures do not detectably track depression or PTSD severity in the studied corpora. Code is available at https://github.com/jen900704/word-aligned-prosody.

papers.title: Homogeneity and heterogeneity of functional element composition of genome units across human and seven model organisms
papers.abstract: Is a chromosome a miniature of its genome, with the same mix of functional elements as the whole? We ask this of eight annotated genomes: human, mouse, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Arabidopsis thaliana and maize. Elements are classified in a four-level hierarchy, from five major classes (protein-coding genes, ncRNA genes, transposable elements (TEs), pseudogenes, IG/TR gene segments) down to finer classes. Units are chromosomes or arms, cytogenetic bands, equal cuts of each chromosome, and random segments of matching size. We compare each unit with the genome and with other units, call compositions homogeneous when they differ by less than 5%, and score each against a random sample of the same size. The first finding is a surprising homogeneity. The level-1 compositions of the major chromosomes match each other and the genome in maize, zebrafish, yeast and C. elegans, and in fly down to the major arms. Finer classes can be homogeneous too: protein function in Arabidopsis, and the Wicker TE orders in maize. Enzyme reaction classes are interchangeable between chromosomes in all eight genomes. The second finding is a structured heterogeneity. Where a unit departs from its genome, it does so in one of three ways: clusters of named elements, such as rRNA genes or immune receptor loci; megabase-scale compartments, such as TE-rich pericentromeric heterochromatin; and lineage-specific gene families, visible only at the finest levels. Corrected for chance, the genomes fall into groups. For protein function and gene families, composition is more uniform in plants and fly than in vertebrates, and least uniform in C. elegans. For the major classes and TE orders, uniformity follows where each genome places its repeats, along the arms (maize, zebrafish) or around the centromeres (Arabidopsis, fly), not its lineage.

papers.title: The Impact of Side Information on Voice Privacy
papers.abstract: Currently, voice-related privacy risks are studied under the assumption that the attacker has access only to spoken audio. In contrast, real-world collections often pair the speech signal with side information; yet to our knowledge, no publicly available dataset provides sufficiently detailed and directly linkable speech and side-information pairs to evaluate the combined risk. We propose a distribution-constrained method to build a semi-synthetic dataset and study singling out risk when geographic side information is assumed to accompany anonymized speech. We instantiate it using the English portion of Mozilla Common Voice and the 2021 UK Census, under ignorant and semi-informed attackers, and introduce a conditional reference that isolates the contribution of the audio beyond the candidate-set reduction induced by the side information. In our controlled geographic case study, for single-utterance speakers, the semi-informed attacker reaches an observed isolation probability of 0.718 in the finest OA-plus-household setting, compared with 0.380 in the signal-only setting; its excess over the conditional reference increases from 0.012 to 0.340. The ignorant attacker shows the same trend at a lower level. The effect is largest at fine granularity and short recordings, precisely the setting in which signal-only evaluation looks safest. Our results show that geographic side information can increase the singling out risk of anonymized speech, and we recommend including attacker settings with side information in future studies of voice privacy.

papers.title: Game-Theoretic Reinforcement Learning based Topology-Agnostic Defense for Virtual Power Plants
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of distributed energy resources (DERs) aggregated by virtual power plants (VPPs) elevates cybersecurity risk by expanding the attack surface. A coordinated cyberattack has the potential to disrupt distribution-system, bulk-system, and market operations. Existing cyberphysical defense strategies largely assume access to grid network models and operating conditions, which may not be available to third-party aggregators. This paper proposes a novel hybrid, perturbation-based cyber-physical defense for VPP-operated DERs that blends game-theoretic planning with model-free reinforcement learning (RL) under a Bayesian belief-update framework. Topology agnosticism is defined from the VPP information and implementation perspective: the VPP does not require access to the feeder topology, line parameters, switching configuration, or full system state. This work advances the state of the art through three contributions: (1) a multi-output Gaussian process with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for discrete attacker-type inference, probability of detection, and confidence of detection for modeling the belief distribution; (2) moment-matched Gaussian propagation of posterior beliefs across episodes; and (3) an RL policy that adaptively integrates Stackelberg leader (VPP) actions with exploration. Furthermore, we establish equilibrium existence and derive an episode-level closed-loop utility bound connecting attacker-belief uncertainty with GT-RL action alignment. Evaluations on IEEE 13- and 123-Bus feeders with DER portfolios demonstrate effective detection under attacker-model uncertainty and evaluated feeder re-configuration conditions, while requiring no explicit feeder-topology knowledge. Overall, the results indicate that combining bi-level game-theoretic planning, nonparametric Bayesian inference, and adaptive RL is a promising direction for VPP cybersecurity.

papers.title: A Symbolic Differentiation_Summation Framework for Power Sums of Arithmetic Sequences
papers.abstract: We give a self-contained derivation of the closed form of the power sums $S_m(n)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_0+(i-1)d)^m$ in which the Bernoulli numbers enter as constants of integration rather than as prescribed coefficients. The derivation rests on an elementary fact: a sum whose terms are polynomial in the index is the restriction to the integers of a unique polynomial, which satisfies the defining difference equation identically and may therefore be differentiated and integrated exactly. Differentiating lowers the power by one; integrating back introduces a single constant, equal to the slope $S_m'(0)$ of the polynomial at the origin and fixed by the value $S_m(1)=a_0^m$. This yields a closed form for $S_m(n)$ in terms of the constants and a recurrence that determines them, obtained without induction on the exponent and without generating functions. With the Bernoulli numbers defined by their classical recurrence, we identify the constants as $d^mB_m(a_0/d)$; the progression starting at $0$ reproduces that recurrence exactly. In the normalized case they are $B_m(1)$, so $C_1=B_1(1)=+\tfrac12$, a value that reflects the summation range; a reflection identity shows, without generating functions, that the odd constants beyond the first vanish. The coefficients of the recurrence are scaled binomial coefficients from a single row of Pascal's triangle, and the same approach gives closed forms for sequences with polynomial differences. The integral recursion behind the method is known in the normalized case; each result is related to its classical counterpart, and a verified implementation is provided.

papers.title: Effective DoF Collapse in Sparse Near-Field Beamforming: A Block-Rank-1 Mechanism
papers.abstract: Sparse near-field arrays phase-cohere $M$ widely separated sub-arrays of $N$ elements and underpin distributed MIMO, satellite formations, and integrated sensing and communication. We show that their interference suppression over a protected region is set by coherence within a single sub-array rather than by the span of the formation: the effective rank of the region covariance can collapse from $MN$ to $M$. Two independent arguments establish this. For canonical line and disk regions each diagonal covariance block is exactly a classical concentration operator, which supplies sharp per-block rank thresholds and makes fewer than one spatial degree of freedom per sub-array a conservative design rule; an orthogonal decomposition with eigenvalue interlacing gives a nonasymptotic sufficient condition that assumes nothing about the coupling between platforms. The consequences are covariance-side and beamformer-independent: the unloaded Capon functional upper-bounds worst-case signal-to-interference ratio, while its regularized counterpart scales very differently for angularly separated and for in-cone targets. An eight-satellite LEO study validates the theory, including realized worst-case SIR.

papers.title: DeltaNet-PC: Test-Time Memory Without Backpropagation Through Time
papers.abstract: Test-time memorization of sequential information is a foundational capability for any intelligent system that needs to rapidly store and retrieve data, as demonstrated by the attention mechanism in large language models. However, Transformers and linear attention variants are trained via backpropagation through time (BPTT), which has drawbacks such as its enormous memory requirements. Predictive coding (PC), an algorithm that optimizes a prediction-error energy function with local updates, offers a compelling solution but still lacks test-time memory for sequential data. We develop a solution to this problem by treating the per-step memory update $ΔS_t$ as a latent variable, as opposed to a slow weight to be learned. By taking the log probability of a standard PC-based probabilistic model, we derive a PC-native solution for verbatim sequence memory, and relate our update rule to common choices in the linear attention literature (e.g., DeltaNet). We present an extensive set of empirical tests to probe our system's properties, including its scaling capacity, memory footprint, and ability to infer a context from evidence (e.g., bank (river) vs. bank (money)). We show how DeltaNet-PC can be used for storing single sequences of data, multiple sequences of data, and key-value associative memory pairs with perfect recall accuracy.

papers.title: SAFE-KV: Causal Suffix Repair for Behavior-Preserving Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in RAG
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reuses the same documents across many requests, making non-prefix KV-cache reuse attractive. Yet a cached document state is not reusable text: it is a context-conditioned causal state whose keys and values depend on the prefix, position, and preceding documents under which it was computed. We formulate non-prefix KV reuse as a behavior-preservation problem with full prefill on the exact prompt as the reference, and introduce SAFE-KV, which repairs a composed cache by re-encoding the causal suffix from a selected start document. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, prefix-conditioned composition preserves only 47.2% of HotpotQA-500 and 37.8% of 2Wiki-500 full-prefill answers; SAFE-KV with risk-guided K2 selection restores 99.8%/98.4% (donor-copy protocol) and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding. Document-only and fixed-window repairs recover far less, because the document states after the repaired region keep histories that omit it. Reuse without repair is exact up to four documents and degrades at sixteen, where suffix repair recovers 98-100%. Faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, so in a single-request L40S study SAFE-KV's operating rule serves every workload by full prefill. SAFE-KV thus establishes the causal-state contract for non-prefix reuse and a validated repair mechanism that meets it.

papers.title: Join Order Enumeration and Optimization for Double-Star and Helix Join Graphs
papers.abstract: Join ordering is classic problem in data management. We highlight the connection between structure-specific dynamic programming algorithms and the mathematical enumeration of the possible merge trees from a join graph. We present two case studies, on double-star and helix shaped join graphs, that we believe carry useful techniques for a toolbox of building structure-specific join optimizers. For the double-star case, we show how the enumeration leads directly to a significantly improved search algorithm, whereas for the helix case we show that a algorithm derived from the mathematical enumeration is not necessarily better than structure-agnostic algorithms.

papers.title: Applications of Royen's Gaussian Correlation Inequality in high-dimensional testing
papers.abstract: Royen's Gaussian Correlation Inequality (GCI) is a fundamental result in statistics and probability, but unfortunately, at least by now, the result is not very well known in the statistical community. In this paper, we demonstrate the potential of GCI in high-dimensional testing problems that involve multivariate Gaussian variables. Leveraging the GCI, we establish sharp Type I error bounds under arbitrary Gaussian covariance structures. We also formulate a conjecture and relate it to the well-known Spherical Cap Covering Conjecture in discrete geometry and Weak Simplex Conjecture in information theory.

papers.title: Interfacial Coupling Reshapes Nonlinear Polarization in a Spin-Defect van der Waals Heterostructure
papers.abstract: Van der Waals heterostructures offer a direct route to couple an optically active layer to a two-dimensional spin sensor, yet their coherent nonlinear response at interfaces remains poorly resolved. Here, we use polarization-resolved second harmonic-generation imaging to resolve four distinct regions of a hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) -based heterostructure, native hBN, neutron-irradiated hBN containing negatively charged boron vacancies (VB-), PbI2 and their complete overlap. The detected intensity scales quadratically with incident power, consistent with a dominant second-order optical process. Polarization scans show that adding PbI2 transforms the distorted VB- SHG anisotropy into a predominantly fourfold response with a sixfold stronger SHG than native hBN alone. This non-additive nonlinear response occurs in the same layer architecture also shown to enhance defect photoluminescence, linking spin-defect sensitization to an interface-modified effective second-order susceptibility.

papers.title: Reparameterizing GFN1-xTB for Ionic Liquids
papers.abstract: Ionic liquids are materials whose properties can be tailored for a wide range of applications, but their chemical diversity and complex electronic structure make systematic screening using quantum-mechanical methods computationally demanding. Semiempirical quantum methods offer an alternative, although their accuracy depends on their parameterization. We investigate the reparameterization of the DFTB method GFN1-xTB for predicting structural, energetic, and electronic properties of ionic liquids. For this purpose, we built a database containing over 14,000 conformations to construct training datasets and explored different parameterization strategies fitted to binding energies, forces, HOMO-LUMO gaps, and geometries. Analysis of the original GFN1-xTB model reveals systematic errors in these properties, with distinct behavior for saturated and aromatic cations. Thus, we investigate two models: CXMIM-xTB, a targeted model trained on imidazolium-based ionic liquids, and IL-xTB, a more general model designed to describe systems containing saturated and aromatic cations. CXMIM-xTB improves the description of binding energies, geometries, and frontier orbital energies while retaining computational efficiency. The model is subsequently applied to estimate electrochemical windows of ionic liquids, providing values consistent with DFT and experimental values. IL-xTB follows a hierarchical parameterization strategy including different cation and anion families and substantially reduces the systematic errors of GFN1-xTB across the chemical space considered, providing a route for developing xTB parameterizations with broader applicability to ionic liquids. Overall, both parameterization strategies outperform the original GFN1-xTB model, demonstrating that reparameterized methods provide an efficient approach for connecting configurational sampling with quantum-mechanical properties of ionic liquids.

papers.title: Continuous Risk-Based Scheduling for Food Safety Inspection: Integrating Historical Decay with Event-Driven Consumer Review Signals
papers.abstract: Batch risk-based inspection scheduling struggles to detect a critical failure class: food facilities with recent clean inspections that subsequently develop severe violations. Traditional systems recompute risk on fixed planning cycles using static historical data, leaving blind spots between inspection cycles. To address this, we introduce the Continuous Inspection Risk (CIR) system, an event-driven scheduling pipeline that re-ranks the inspection queue dynamically as new data arrives. CIR combines a decay-weighted historical score with a stream of real-time consumer reviews triaged by a language-model classifier. A key structural contribution is our temporal partition rule, which strictly excludes reviews predating the most recent inspection to prevent superseded signals from skewing current risk. Evaluating CIR on 9,505 routine inspections in Santa Clara County, California (2024-2026), we show that history-based scoring alone reduces mean time-to-detection of major violations by 69 days (20.9%) under a 30% inspection budget, but fails to anticipate severe vermin-related closures (0/8 detected). Incorporating post-inspection review signals drastically improves performance, predicting 7 of 8 vermin closures with an average lead time of 117 days-firing on the exact day of review publication in four instances. Introducing a review corroboration rule improves precision from 0.70 to 0.78 without loss of recall. Finally, we analyze critical implementation challenges, documenting a data-hygiene pitfall (stale review leakage across inspection boundaries) and an evaluation limitation involving unobserved facility self-remediation. This work provides the first case-level evaluation of event-driven inspection triggering using open data and provides a reproducible benchmark for review-augmented public health systems

papers.title: Directivity Estimates and Tolerance Tradeoffs in the Presence of Random Perturbations
papers.abstract: The practicality of realizing high-directivity sources is studied using a generalized sensitivity metrics. These measures are based on the error model adopted in previous studies on array tolerance, but account for heterogeneous array characteristics in an arbitrary source-expansion basis, making it applicable to the study of continuous sources, ideal uncoupled arrays, and heterogeneous arrays with mutual coupling. The formulation provides the ensemble average of realized directivity under the selected error model, making it a fast predictor of anticipated directivity reduction due to source perturbation. The data required to compute these predictions are straightforward to obtain via simulation or measurement, with a significant simplification when the system can be approximated as lossless. The directivity and the proposed tolerance measures allow for the formulation of optimization problems illustrating the tradeoff between these measures. Several examples demonstrate these tradeoffs, special cases, comparison to previous estimates of maximum directivity, and the accuracy of sensitivity as a predictor of statistical performance over large ensembles of design realizations.

papers.title: Programmable Data Layouts via On-The-Fly Data Transformation
papers.abstract: The performance of modern computing systems is heavily bottlenecked by the widening gap between processing throughput and main memory latency, a problem exacerbated when an application's logical data access patterns misalign with the physical layout of data in memory. To address this, we propose a hardware-software co-design framework comprising the Data Transformation Language (DTL) and the Data Transformation Unit (DTU). DTL allows programmers to concisely express complex data layout reorganizations, which the compiler translates into efficient hardware routing configurations. The DTU, a hardware engine logically situated between the Last-Level Cache (LLC) and main memory, transparently evaluates these configurations on-the-fly to gather scattered data elements into dense, logically contiguous cache lines. By converting explicit layout transformations into virtual views, this approach eliminates the need for explicit data materialization in software. We evaluate the DTU within a quad-core RISC-V SoC using FireSim, demonstrating substantial improvements in execution speed and memory efficiency.

papers.title: Precision follows the decision: how well an acceptance probability is known for mean-spread release rules
papers.abstract: Many release rules accept a lot when a statistic built from the sample mean and standard deviation stays within a limit, and the probability that a process passes such a rule can be computed exactly for a broad class of parent distributions. This paper asks how well that probability is itself known once the parent has been estimated. Under a stated reference posterior the answer is an interval, narrow where a lot clearly passes or fails and wide where it is contested. In ninety-eight published content-uniformity lots that position, not the sample size, sets the width: among the forty-eight lots assayed at the same ten units, and so equally informed about the spread, the $95\%$ interval runs from essentially zero width to $0.96$. With the operating point held fixed while test and estimation sample grow together, the interval narrows only slowly, the contraction of the posterior being offset by the steepening of the operating characteristic; a calibrated study at the sample sizes of $1207$ occupational exposure assessments shows the same under a half-plane rule. For a pure-spread rule under a Normal parent the interval has an exact chi-square form in the plug-in value and the two sample sizes, extending to the mean-spread wedge with a measured residual and containing Bergum's lower bound as one endpoint. With the parent's posterior formed from the same published summaries through the evaluator's own likelihood, the qualitative pattern survives but shape moves both endpoints and width: on the same lots a strong right skew lowers the pessimistic endpoint by up to a fifth and widens the interval by up to $0.22$. At the content-uniformity operating point studied, under a Normal parent, the symmetric error bar in standard use puts the lower endpoint $0.21$ too high and returns an upper endpoint above one, even with the full posterior covariance.

papers.title: Extremals for singular Onofri type inequality in weighted Sobolev spaces
papers.abstract: The $N$-dimensional Euclidean Onofri inequality was proved by Del Pino and Dolbeault for smooth compactly supported functions in $\mathbb{R}^N$ with $N \ge 2$. In this paper, we consider the singular version introduced by Lam and Lu, and extend it to a natural weighted Sobolev space. Next, we establish a sharp singular Carleson-Chang type inequality and prove its equivalence with the singular $N$-dimensional Euclidean Onofri inequality. Furthermore, we prove the existence of nontrivial, non-constant optimizers for the functional associated with the singular Euclidean Onofri inequality, answering open questions left by Del Pino and Dolbeault in the non-singular case, and by Lam and Lu in the case with singularities. To this end, we exploit the classification result obtained for a singular Liouville-type equation involving the $N$-Laplacian. We also prove the conformal invariance of the functional, establish the sharpness of the singular $N$-dimensional Euclidean Onofri inequality in terms of optimal constants, and state several consequences, including a sharp Poincaré inequality.

papers.title: Nucleation at the GST--oxide interface and beam-driven ordering in amorphous Ge--Sb--Te: HAADF, EDS and electron pair distribution functions across a 4D-STEM dose series
papers.abstract: Where crystal nuclei form in amorphous phase-change materials decides how they switch. We study six successive 4D-STEM scans, with simultaneous HAADF and EDS data, of a magnetron-sputtered Ge-Sb-Te (GST) film, restricted to the GST layer and its interface with the oxide beneath it. Nucleation sites do not differ in composition or number density: the nuclei lie on the same robust HAADF-EDS relation as the matrix, and at fixed HAADF the spread of the summed EDS signal equals its Poisson counting noise (ratio 1.03 +- 0.05). The nuclei are nevertheless crystalline and stand out in the 4D-STEM max-intensity virtual image (median z = 11.0) but not in HAADF (z = 1.3) or EDS (z = 0.3). We classify the film in four ways (HAADF intensity, I(q) phase mapping, PCA of the whole diffraction patterns and a self-supervised SimCLR encoder) and compare the electron pair distribution functions (PDFs) of all classes after calibrating reciprocal space on the Au cap. All bulk classes share one short-range structure (first shell 2.70-2.74 Å); towards the interface the first sharp diffraction peak (FSDP) moves to lower q, and every method isolates a thin interface-edge environment with a shorter or missing first shell. The I(q) classification isolates, in every scan, an interface environment that holds 62-100% of the nucleus pixels (1.2-2.5-fold above depth) and persists when the nucleus pixels are removed before classification. The interface, rather than a distinct composition or density of the nucleating volume, therefore marks where nuclei form. Over 4.7e3 e/Å^2 the HAADF signal falls by 17%, the first shell shortens by 0.03 Å and the FSDP narrows by 9%, apparently ordering the film as it damages it. All analyses used PySTEMLab, an interactive 4D-STEM analysis environment developed for this work.

papers.title: Superlattice-Stabilized Fractional Chern Insulators in a "Berry Basin" Model
papers.abstract: The discovery of integer and fractional Chern insulators in rhombohedral graphene, following their discovery in the isolated topological flat band in twisted MoTe$_2$, motivates a search for the conditions under which an electronic band can host a topological correlated state. In this Letter we introduce a ``Berry basin" model which captures the essential features of rhombohedral graphene: a dispersive band with a flat bottom, momentum-space winding of a ``layer" degree of freedom, and Coulomb interactions, while also including periodic potentials, enabling controlled studies of the interplay of quantum geometry, superlattice modulation, and electron-electron interactions in producing correlated topological states beyond the isolated topological band paradigm. While integer Chern insulators emerge at strong coupling without a superlattice potential, stabilizing the fractional state requires nonzero potential for all interaction strengths we access. We provide insight into the greater robustness of integer and fractional Chern insulators in rhombohedral graphene when electrons are polarized away from the moiré interface. Our results establish a new class of systems that host robust fractional Chern insulators and provide a controlled numerical platform to test competing theories of interacting topological phases.

papers.title: On the Effectiveness of NetFlow-Based Deanonymization of Tor Onion Services (Extended Version)
papers.abstract: In the context of Tor, deanonymization attacks via traffic correlation have long been studied for both clients and onion services. Complementing prior investigations that utilize fine-grained flow metadata such as packet sizes and timings, we study a relatively less explored yet easier-to-obtain adversarial capability: deanonymization using only coarse NetFlow-style telemetry, such as one-minute, 1-out-of-1,000 sampled packet counts. We first revisit active NetFlow-based traffic analysis attacks against Tor onion services and show, through large-scale experiments with live Tor data, that coarse telemetry is sufficient to deanonymize a targeted onion service when the adversary can induce discernible traffic patterns through controlled downloads. We then introduce a stronger active attack based on controlled introduction requests, which removes application-specific assumptions and gives adversaries more flexibility while achieving comparable success rates. Finally, we present a passive deanonymization attack that sends zero traffic to target onion services. The attack exploits Tor's puzzle-based DoS defense as a side channel: public puzzle difficulty reveals service-load changes that can be semantically matched against NetFlow traces. Our findings show that coarse network telemetry poses a practical deanonymization threat to onion services today and call for proactive mitigations and a redesign of the globally visible defense signals that may leak service-load information.

papers.title: The Rényi area law conjecture is false below $α=1$ in high dimensions
papers.abstract: Area laws express the expectation that entanglement in gapped quantum ground states scales with a boundary rather than a volume. In one dimension this holds for every Rényi entropy, and the Rényi area-law conjecture asserts the same in higher dimensions for each fixed $0<α<1$. Here we disprove this conjecture in every spatial dimension two and higher. We construct finite-range Hamiltonians with fixed local dimension, bounded interaction strength, unique ground states and a uniform spectral gap, whose ground states exhibit volume-law Rényi entanglement while obeying a von Neumann area law and remaining connected to product states through uniformly gapped local paths. The mechanism is error-space complexity: locally identifiable components of arbitrarily small weight can encode states with high entanglement complexity. We also establish the worst-case rank-error trade-off for approximate ground-state projectors, a key tool in one-dimensional area-law proofs. At fixed gap, the optimal Schmidt rank at projection error $ε$ across a planar cut of cross-section $A$ scales as $\exp[\tildeΘ((A\logε^{-1})^{2/3})]$ when $\logε^{-1}\gtrsim A$. Thus $α=1$ is the sharp threshold for a universal Rényi area law within this adiabatically connected class.

papers.title: Local Suppression of Superconductivity in Niobium Films by Focused Silicon Ion Implantation
papers.abstract: Magnetic flux trapped in a superconducting circuit shifts the critical currents of nearby Josephson junctions and disturbs the operation of the circuit. The usual remedy is a moat etched through the ground plane to hold the flux away from the logic. We report direct write silicon ion implantation with a focused ion beam as a way to make moats without etching the film, by locally suppressing superconductivity in niobium (Nb). Single implanted lines were written across Nb electrodes in films of three thicknesses over two orders of magnitude in ion fluence, and the transition temperature, resistance, and critical current density of each line were measured. The transition temperature of the line falls with fluence while the surrounding Nb is unchanged, and the critical current density falls by about two orders of magnitude before the line becomes resistive at 4.2 K. The product of the critical current and the resistance of the lines follows a single power law in reduced temperature. This gives an estimate of the critical current of a line at any temperature from its transition temperature and resistance. A time dependent Ginzburg-Landau simulation indicates that an implanted region can capture and hold a vortex. From these results we suggest a starting ion energy and fluence for implanted moats in a 100 nm Nb ground plane at 4.2 K and estimate the equivalent broad beam fluence.

papers.title: Selection of Marginally Stable Patterns by Boundary Conditions
papers.abstract: We study the effect of boundary conditions on the selection of wavenumbers in pattern-forming systems. Prior work established that, for a large class of boundary conditions, equilibria only within a narrow band of wavenumbers are compatible with the boundary. We demonstrate here that for a large class of initial conditions, solutions evolve towards an extremal member of this narrow band of equilibria. In fact, this extremal member is neutrally stable, nonlinearly unstable, and the convergence is realized through a series of snapping events at the boundary. We observe this behavior in simulations of the Swift-Hohenberg equation when the pattern forming region is confined to a large spatial interval through a parameter quench. We prove the convergence in a phase-diffusion approximation using comparison principles and astutely chosen subsolutions that mimic the snapping behavior.

papers.title: Adaptive two-points zero-order accelerated methods for stochastic convex optimization problems
papers.abstract: We study stochastic convex optimization, where each sampled function can be evaluated at two arbitrary points. Our accelerated method chooses step sizes, batch sizes and smoothing radii from function values. A forward difference between smoothing scales controls the radius; we account for changes in the smoothed objective. Under the stated regularity and second-moment assumptions, exact function evaluations give \begin{multline*} \mathbb{E}\bigl[f(x_N)-f(x^\star)\bigr] \le \widetilde{O}\biggl( \frac{\sqrt{d}\,M_2 D}{\sqrt{T}} +\min\biggl( \frac{L D^2}{N^2},\; \frac{d^{1/4} M D}{N}+\frac{\sqrt{d}\,M D^2}{γ_{\max} N^2} \biggr)\biggr). \end{multline*} Here $N,T,d,D$ denote the numbers of optimization steps and paired evaluations, the dimension and a feasible-set diameter bound, respectively. Evaluations are available within Euclidean distance $γ_{\max}$ of the feasible set. For the population objective $f(x)=\mathbb{E}_ξ F(x,ξ)$, $M$ satisfies $|f(x)-f(y)|\le M\|x-y\|_2$, and $M_2$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}_ξ\|\nabla F(x,ξ)\|_2^2\le M_2^2$ for sample weak gradients in the interior of the evaluation domain. The method requires no $L,M,M_2$, where $L$ is a Lipschitz constant of $\nabla f$; set $L=+\infty$ without smoothness. The method uses exactly $2T$ values in $3N$ sequential sampling rounds with predetermined batches, or $5N$ with batches chosen from observations. An extension selects a search radius without a supplied distance bound. Fixed radius parameters can leave nonvanishing error; suitable choices depending on the budgets yield convergence.

papers.title: Do LLMs differentiate linguistic traits internally?: A layer-wise analysis
papers.abstract: Large language models often produce judgments that resemble human responses, but it remains unclear whether they internally capture linguistic nuances such as conventional versus idiomatic meaning. A layer-wise representational analysis was conducted on two equal-sized pre-trained models, Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-3-1B-PT, to examine whether and where these models differentiate linguistic traits from input. The analysis combined layer-wise probing with geometric distance measures, using the top embedding dimensions ranked by principal component loadings for each layer. The results show that even with equal capacity, models organize linguistic information in fundamentally different ways, suggesting the need to analyze internal representational geometry, examining not just behavioral outputs but semantic space alignment when evaluating how closely human and model language interpretation correspond.

papers.title: SocraticRepair: Planning-Guided Socratic Tutoring for Program Debugging and Misconception Repair
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in computer science education. However, the teaching abilities of even the most powerful LLMs are limited: they tend to reveal the solution prematurely and may lose focus on the learner's current debugging objective. To address this, we introduce SocraticRepair, a planning-guided Socratic tutoring framework for program debugging and miscon- ception repair that adapts prior planning-guided tutoring work (Li et al., 2026b). The framework is instantiated in the Python programming domain by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on synthetic multi-turn tutoring dialogues constructed from four preprocessed programming datasets. The system is evaluated using a predefined set of independent metrics and benchmarked against a general-purpose LLM. The experiments show that SocraticRepair achieves higher scores on stepwise scaffolding and question quality while also substantially reducing premature solution disclosure. The results also identify reliable pedagogical plan generation as an important remaining challenge.

papers.title: MoSAIC: Learning DAG Scheduling Heuristics from Optimal Schedules through Motif-Aware Recovery and LLM-Guided Reasoning
papers.abstract: Efficient task scheduling in heterogeneous computing systems remains a fundamental challenge in embedded and high-level synthesis flows. This paper presents MoSAIC (Motif-aware Scheduling with AI-driven Cognition), a learning-based framework that bridges the gap between exact and heuristic scheduling approaches for DAG-based applications. The system uses the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to learn the relationships between DAG structures and scheduling priority functions. The framework first leverages the OR-Tools CP-SAT solver [4] to generate optimal schedules, which are then used to supervise the learning of compact priority-based scheduling functions through Bayesian Optimization. These learned heuristics capture relationships between scheduling decisions and structural graph features such as rank, depth, and fanout, enabling the construction of a reusable knowledge base across diverse DAG instances. Experimental results across synthetic graph families and real-world benchmarks, including PolyBench and MachSuite, show that the learned heuristics consistently improve over classical approaches such as HEFT [2], while maintaining low runtime overhead. The results indicate that combining optimal supervision with learning-based generalization provides a practical approach for scalable and adaptive task scheduling.

papers.title: A computer-assisted proof of Krzyż's conjecture for the sixth coefficient
papers.abstract: We develop a computer-assisted approach to Krzyż's conjecture based on validated elimination of the masses in an extremal Herglotz representation. The entropy theorem of Lei and Zhang, together with the Agler--McCarthy reduction, leaves only extremals with fewer than $n$ atoms to exclude. In the critical stratum with $n-1$ atoms, the first-order conditions are linear in the masses. Validated local inversion reduces the regular search to $n$ outer parameters, with a rank-free fallback at singular configurations. This gives a proof of the sixth-coefficient conjecture, including its equality statement; the critical-stratum computation takes 8.2 minutes on an M4 Pro. We also obtain an independent proof for the seventh coefficient, recently established by Xie. The computational exclusions use explicit rounding-error bounds, and the equality cases follow analytically.

papers.title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking

papers.title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
papers.abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.

papers.title: Cosmology & Astrophysics of the Dark Dimension with Bulk Majorana Neutrinos
papers.abstract: Recently, the possibility of having sterile Majorana neutrinos charged under $B-L$ gauge symmetry in the bulk of the dark dimension has been explored. We point out a cosmological restriction on the Majorana mass of bulk neutrinos leading to mass $\gtrsim 100~{\rm GeV}$. This avoids the over-production of Kaluza-Klein neutrino towers in the early universe thus resolving the cosmological neutrino catastrophe of extra dimension scenarios. If the mass of the bulk neutrino is at the lower end of this bound, it can potentially also explain the recently observed Fermi halo excess on gamma rays through the evaporation of long-lived 5d (i.e. dark) black holes through Hawking radiation to bulk neutrinos, which promptly decay into standard model particles.

papers.title: Signal-to-noise problems in fault-tolerant quantum computation
papers.abstract: Quantum computation offers a promising alternative to classical Monte Carlo methods by naturally avoiding sign problems through unitary evolution. A common misconception follows from this: because quantum simulation sidesteps the sign problem, it is often assumed to be an essentially perfect substitute for classical sampling. This is false---quantum measurements are intrinsically stochastic, and estimating observables often requires a number of samples that grows exponentially with system size, time separation, or inverse temperature, exactly as in the classical signal-to-noise problem. In this work, we analyze the origin and structure of signal-to-noise problems in quantum computation, drawing parallels with classical Monte Carlo, and demonstrate that such noise persists even in sign-problem-free regimes. We discuss strategies to mitigate it, in particular a quantum generalization of Stein control variates construction, in which unbiased estimators are built from operator commutators $[X,A]$ and their discrete diagonal counterparts, and validate the approach with exactly solvable numerical examples that quantify the achievable variance reduction. Our results underscore that variance reduction, not merely sign-problem avoidance, is required to make quantum algorithms practically viable for many-body physics.

papers.title: NAS Timers for Non-Terrestrial Networks: Current Standards and Directions
papers.abstract: Response-supervision timers in the 5G Non-Access Stratum (NAS) bound the time allowed for signaling exchanges before retransmission or abnormal-case handling begins. In non-terrestrial networks, that interval can include satellite propagation, terrestrial transport, and processing by multiple core-network functions. Under current 3GPP specifications, the applicable timer value for satellite access is selected according to the satellite NG-RAN radio access technology (RAT) type. However, control paths within the same low Earth orbit (LEO) network can differ in propagation delay and processing load. This article reviews the relevant 3GPP timer semantics and traces the delay components covered by different timers through 5G registration. It organizes candidate refinements along two dimensions: configuration granularity and information scope. A registration case study illustrates the trade-off between avoiding premature timer expiry and recovering promptly from message loss. The article identifies the information and coordination that future specifications would need to address to support interoperable timer configuration.

papers.title: Stable Causal Estimation with Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: In observational studies, the overlap assumption, also called positivity, is frequently strained in practice. Limited overlap destabilizes widely used estimators such as inverse propensity weighting (IPW), whose variance depends on density ratios that explode as propensity scores approach zero or one. To address this challenge, we propose the Stable Transport Estimator (STE), an optimal transport-based approach for estimating average causal effects when overlap holds but strict overlap fails. Unlike IPW, the variance of STE contains no density-ratio factor; it is governed by the transport map itself and stays finite under bounded moments, even when density ratios diverge. By replacing reweighting with a geometry-aware transport map, STE constructs stable counterfactual comparisons without requiring density estimation or propensity score modeling. STE further extends to settings where the overlap condition is violated: when covariate supports overlap only partially, a linear interpolation transport map enables principled extrapolation with explicit bias-variance trade-offs. We establish consistency, asymptotic normality, and a variance characterization that makes explicit the contribution of the estimated transport map to the asymptotic variance. Across synthetic and real datasets, STE demonstrates improved robustness, reduced bias, and markedly more stable variance compared to existing estimators.

papers.title: Validation of Space Weather Forecasting at Leonid Space
papers.abstract: We validate Leonid Space's space weather forecasts through comprehensive cross-validation of retroforecasts scored against the entire F10.7 and Ap historical record. We built a unified forecast model that jointly forecasts F10.7 and Ap on all timescales from 3 hours up to multi-decade chains of future solar cycles. This was used to generate an archive of historical 15-year retroforecasts, after performing a leave-one-out fit of the model on held-out data and conditioning only on historical data available at the time. The accuracy of this archive was scored against measured space weather indices at all lookahead horizons from 1 day to 15 years, using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) as the primary quality metric. All other publicly available F10.7 and Ap forecast archives were scored using the same approach, including NASA's MSAFE and Schatten forecasts, SWPC's 27-day, 45-day, and Solar Cycle predictions, SWPC/USAF's RSGA, SIDC's Ursigram, CLS, Athens, KSO, BGS, SEPC's 3-day and 27-day forecasts, AFRL/NSO's SIFT, and BoM. Taken together, these 15 flux forecasts and 12 Ap forecasts compared on common lookahead metrics make up the most comprehensive cross-comparison of space weather forecasts we are aware of. Over a common forecast interval since 2000, Leonid had the lowest CRPS prediction error of any F10.7 or Ap prediction model: strictly lowest for Ap at all lookaheads and for F10.7 up to 5 years, and parity with MSAFE after 5 years. Much of this performance comes from our well-calibrated uncertainty bands, and we urge space weather forecasters to include calibrated uncertainties with their predictions and to issue retroforecast archives that can be used to rigorously evaluate their generating models.

papers.title: Transition-Metal Chalcogenide Nanowires: A First-Principles Study of Stability, Electronic Structure, and Mechanical Response
papers.abstract: Subnanometer transition-metal chalcogenide nanowires provide a one-dimensional platform in which electronic functionality and mechanical response can be tuned through chemical composition. Here, density functional theory calculations are combined with machine-learning force-field (MLFF) molecular dynamics to investigate MoS, MoSe, MoTe, WS, WSe, and WTe nanowires. The optimized structures are dynamically stable within the harmonic approximation, and their electronic character evolves systematically across the chalcogen series: MoS, MoSe, WS, and WSe are metallic, whereas MoTe and WTe are semiconducting, with HSE06 band gaps of 0.52 and 0.20 eV, respectively. The effective axial stiffness decreases from sulfides to selenides and tellurides, consistent with the increase in metal--chalcogen bond length; using a circular effective cross section, the corresponding Young moduli range from 392 to 718 GPa. All six nanowires have negative formation energies relative to the selected elemental reference phases. MLFF trajectories extending to 2.5 ns at 300 K preserve the one-dimensional morphology and local atomic order, providing evidence of finite-temperature dynamical stability on the simulated time scale. The corresponding MLFF molecular-dynamics energy traces are shown in. We further examine the response of the nanowires to axial strain and curvature, including strain-induced band-gap modulation in the tellurides. These results establish composition and mechanical deformation as complementary routes for tuning the electronic and mechanical properties of ultrathin transition-metal chalcogenide nanowires and support their further investigation as components of flexible nanoelectronic systems.

papers.title: nanoflann: A Header-Only KD-Tree Library for Exact Nearest-Neighbor Search on Compile-Time Product Manifolds
papers.abstract: Nearest-neighbor (NN) search underlies countless robotics algorithms, but many state spaces are not Euclidean: orientations live on $SO(2)$ or $SO(3)$ and poses on $SE(2)$ or $SE(3)$, and a Euclidean KD-tree on their raw coordinates returns wrong neighbors. We present a header-only, dependency-free C++ KD-tree library for exact NN search on user-defined product manifolds declared at compile time: the space is composed from base manifolds ($\mathbb{R}^n$, $SO(2)$, $SO(3)$, $S^n$; products $SE(2)$, $SE(3)$, tori) with a single type alias, and the library synthesizes a metric whose pruning is provably admissible, wrap-aware for circular coordinates and double-cover-aware for unit quaternions. Experiments confirm exactness (recall $1.0$ vs an exhaustive scan under the same product metric), where the Euclidean-on-raw shortcut collapses to recall $\approx 0.5^{m}$ for $m$ rotation blocks, with up to three orders of magnitude speedup over brute force. We further contribute an incremental, self-balancing single-tree index for points under heavy churn (e.g. sliding-window LiDAR maps) or $SE(3)$ trajectories: bounded memory and faster updates than prior work, with an optional asynchronous tail-latency-bounding mode. The implementation is open source: https://github.com/jlblancoc/nanoflann

papers.title: Polynomial mixing for infinite-energy solutions of the white-forced Navier--Stokes equation in an infinite pipe
papers.abstract: We study the long-time behavior of the infinite-energy solutions to the white-forced Navier--Stokes equation in an infinite pipe $\mathbb{R}\times (-1,1)$ with no-slip boundary conditions. The equation is globally well-posed in uniformly local spaces satisfying the divergence-free condition. Under suitable degeneracy and spatial decay assumptions on the noise, we prove the uniqueness of the invariant measure and establish polynomial mixing in the dual-Lipschitz metric. This provides an affirmative answer to Open Problem 1 posed by Kuksin and Shirikyan \cite{KS17} in the case of zero cross-sectional flux.

papers.title: A counterexample to Vaught's Conjecture for $L_{ω_1,ω}$
papers.abstract: We construct a sentence of $L_{ω_1,ω}$ having exactly $\aleph_1$ many countable models up to isomorphism, but no perfect set of non-isomorphic models. This disproves Vaught's conjecture for infinitary logic. The construction follows a framework devised by Robin Knight, and the proof has been formally verified in Lean.

papers.title: Running Fewer Loops Removes Refusal Behaviour in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
papers.abstract: A recurrent-depth language model reuses one block of weights several times in a row. The number of repetitions, which we call loops, is chosen when the model runs, not when it is trained, and running fewer is cheaper and faster, so a deployment may choose to do it. Running fewer loops also makes these models less safe, and the loss of safety is larger than the loss of anything else we measured. We study four released Ouro checkpoints and Huginn-0125. At half of its trained depth, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking still solves 0.692 of the GSM8K maths problems, against 0.775 at full depth, keeping 89% of its accuracy. Over the same reduction, the rate at which it helps with harmful requests rises from 0.038 to 0.205, 5.3 times higher. The information is not lost: a linear classifier reads whether a request is harmful from the model's internal state after a single loop, with an ROC AUC of 0.967 against 0.986 at full depth. What the missing loops remove is the refusal that should follow. We measure the effect with four instruments, one generating no text at all, and reproduce it on a second model family. Removing a single direction from Ouro-1.4B's internal state at full depth drops its refusal rate on harmful prompts from 0.950 to 0.130, identifying what the shallow model is missing. Two run-time repairs do not help: the models' early-exit rules do not spend more loops on harmful requests, and choosing a depth per request does not recover the loss. Changing the training does. Standard safety training makes the shallow model safe only by refusing 0.865 of harmless requests, while training at randomly chosen depths reaches a separation of +0.399 between harmful and harmless refusal at one loop, against +0.118. On Huginn-0125 it keeps harmful help at or below 0.040 at every depth from 1 to 32 loops, where standard training reaches 0.194, and it costs no accuracy at full depth.

papers.title: Non-Intrusive Balancing for Data-Driven Model Reduction with Oblique Projections
papers.abstract: Non-intrusive reduced-order modeling is essential for systems simulated with black- or gray-box solvers, yet computing accurate data-driven models remains challenging when the dynamics exhibit large-amplitude transient energy growth. This is because state-of-the-art non-intrusive methods typically rely on orthogonal projection onto high-energy linear or nonlinear manifolds identified by minimizing static reconstruction losses, which truncates low-energy, yet dynamically important, states. Intrusive methods such as Balanced Truncation and its extensions address this issue by using adjoint information to define dynamics-aware oblique projections. Here, we show that balancing-based oblique projections for nonlinear systems can instead be computed non-intrusively from forward simulation data. Specifically, we develop a framework to compute the nonlinear empirical reachability Gramian and balance it against its observability counterpart, projected onto a suitable restriction subspace. This procedure provably recovers the oblique projection of Balanced Truncation when the dynamics are linear and the range of either Gramian is contained in the restriction subspace. Moreover, in the linear case and in the absence of adjoint information, we show that the minimax-optimal restriction subspace spans the dominant eigenspaces of the reachability Gramian, which informs an efficient balancing algorithm with cost comparable to a standard SVD. Once the oblique projection is computed, we use Operator Inference to learn the latent-space dynamics on its range. The method is demonstrated on several examples of increasing complexity, including the three-dimensional incompressible flow past a wing with $8\times 10^7$ degrees of freedom. In all examples, the Balanced Operator Inference models significantly outperform their POD-based counterparts, reducing forecasting error by up to two orders of magnitude.

papers.title: Residual-based error control for neural Galerkin reconstruction of minimum-norm wave controls
papers.abstract: We analyse how errors in independently approximated adjoint waves propagate into the Hilbert Uniqueness Method (HUM) reconstruction of the minimum-$L^2$-norm interior control of a variable-coefficient wave equation. The central result is an identity: the error of the control assembled exactly from any approximate adjoints splits orthogonally into the distance of the minimum-norm control to their observation span and a moment-inconsistency term generated by their interior wave residuals. From it we derive a posteriori bounds for the returned control, including assembly and solve errors, and a continuous accept-or-refine test for the network directions returned by training; under continuous observability, a fully discrete estimate separates truncation, adjoint and assembly errors. The adjoints are computed here by adaptive Galerkin neural networks, but the bounds apply to any computed adjoints. In one-dimensional benchmarks with known minimum-norm controls, all inputs are enclosed by ball arithmetic. Without truncation the residual bounds exceed the true error by factors of 9 to 115; with sixteen adjoints outside the trial class, a truncated terminal space and all inputs computed from the target data, by about 1.08 to 6.50. In two and three dimensions, including a time-dependent coefficient, the neural controls closely reproduce reference controls of the same truncation, and at equal neuron counts trained hidden features reduce the error more than tenfold relative to random features. Classical solvers are much cheaper in all tested cases, and certification is confined to the one-dimensional benchmarks.

papers.title: HarnessNet: Feedback-driven Hierarchical Joint Harness Evolution for Multi-agent Systems
papers.abstract: AI agents can evolve by using environment feedback to revise their harnesses, the software managing model inputs, tool use, memory, and execution, while keeping foundation models frozen. Existing studies focus on single agents, leaving joint harness evolution in multi-agent systems (MAS) underexplored. A single global optimizer faces growing context and workload as the system scales, while access restrictions may prevent sharing agent internals or system-wide feedback. We propose HarnessNet, a framework for hierarchical harness evolution in MAS. Its basic unit, Agentron, comprises an evolvable forward harness, a foundation model, and a local optimizer that can observe and modify only that harness. Agentrons form a layered graph through which environment feedback propagates backward, with upstream optimizers receiving node-specific feedback from the downstream layer. This decomposes joint harness evolution into smaller, coordinated tasks with separate contexts, reducing individual optimizers' context and workload while keeping access local.
